subject: Pathology
stem:
Match each condition with its iron profile.

| Condition | Profile |
|---|---|
| 1. Iron-deficiency anaemia | a. Ferritin raised, TIBC low, transferrin saturation low |
| 2. Anaemia of chronic disease | b. Ferritin normal, iron studies normal, HbA₂ raised |
| 3. β-thalassaemia trait | c. Ferritin raised, transferrin saturation raised, ring sideroblasts |
| 4. Sideroblastic anaemia | d. Ferritin low, TIBC raised, transferrin saturation low |
explanation: Ferritin is the best single test for iron deficiency, but it is an acute-phase reactant and rises in inflammation. In anaemia of chronic disease, iron is plentiful but locked away in macrophages.

explanation: Mentzer index = MCV ÷ RBC count (millions) = 64 ÷ 5.8 ≈ 11. Below 13 suggests thalassaemia trait, where many small red cells are made; above 13 suggests iron deficiency. Confirm with HbA₂ by HPLC.

options: Hepcidin, induced by IL-6, which degrades ferroportin
explanation: Ferroportin is the only cellular iron exporter. Without it, both gut absorption and release from macrophages are blocked. Iron overload also raises hepcidin, while hypoxia and active erythropoiesis (via erythroferrone) lower it.

explanation: EMA binds band 3; spherocytes show reduced fluorescence. Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects of ankyrin, spectrin, band 3 or protein 4.2, is mostly autosomal dominant, and characteristically has a raised MCHC. A negative DAT helps rule out autoimmune haemolysis.

stem: Which statement about paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is FALSE?

Cells lack GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59
Thrombosis, especially of hepatic and abdominal veins, is the main cause of death
It is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern
explanation: PIGA is on the X chromosome, but the mutation is acquired, not inherited. That is why PNH is "the haemolytic anaemia that is not inherited" (an intracorpuscular yet acquired defect). Flow cytometry (CD55/CD59, FLAER) is the gold standard. Eculizumab blocks C5.

explanation: In cold agglutinin disease, the IgM antibody binds red cells in cool peripheral blood, fixes complement and then falls off on warming, leaving only C3d. explanation: An excess of membrane cholesterol produces irregular spiky cells, which the spleen destroys. Acanthocytes are also seen in abetalipoproteinaemia, McLeod phenotype and neuroacanthocytosis (PKAN). Echinocytes ("burr cells") have regular short spines.

| Lymphoma | Translocation |
|---|---|
| 1. Follicular lymphoma | a. t(11;18) API2–MALT1 |
| 2. Mantle cell lymphoma | b. t(14;18) IGH–BCL2 |
| 3. Gastric MALT lymphoma not responding to H. pylori eradication | c. t(8;14) MYC–IGH |

stem:
Match each platelet disorder with its laboratory feature.

| Disorder | Feature |
|---|---|
| 1. Bernard–Soulier syndrome | a. No aggregation with ADP, collagen or epinephrine; normal ristocetin response |
| 2. Glanzmann thrombasthenia | b. Absent ristocetin response that corrects with normal plasma |
| 3. von Willebrand disease | c. Giant platelets, thrombocytopenia, absent ristocetin response not corrected by plasma |

stem: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of apoptosis and NOT of necrosis?

A "ladder" of DNA fragments in multiples of about 180–200 bp
Release of cell contents with inflammation
explanation: Caspase-activated DNase cuts DNA between nucleosomes. Apoptotic cells shrink, keep their membranes intact, show phosphatidylserine for phagocytosis, and cause no inflammation. Enzyme activation occurs in both forms of death, so it does not separate them.

| 2. Necroptosis | b. One live cell invades and dies inside another |
| 3. Ferroptosis | c. Caspase-1 activated by the inflammasome, releasing IL-1β |

options: Low IgM, with high IgA and IgE
